name: Spanish
intro: The main examples use broadly standard Spanish with Spain-oriented notes and explicit Latin American comparisons. Learn both vosotros recognition and ustedes usage, and later regional voseo where relevant. Spanish-speaking communities differ in pronunciation, vocabulary and pragmatic conventions. Standard grammar knowledge should support broad comprehension rather than erase regional identity.

foundation.name: Spanish
notes: Ñ is a letter after N. ch and ll are digraphs, not separate letters in current alphabetical ordering. Letter names for b/v/w/y vary regionally. h is normally silent; j is a fricative whose realisation varies.

The five vowel phonemes are relatively stable. In much of Spain, c before e/i and z give /θ/; across Latin America and other regions they give /s/. b and v do not form the English /b/ versus /v/ contrast. ll/y pronunciation varies regionally.

Without an accent, words ending in a vowel, n or s normally stress the penultimate syllable; other endings normally stress the final syllable. Written accents override this: teléfono, café. Accent marks also distinguish some grammatical words: tú/tu, él/el, sí/si.
building: el libro nuevo → los libros nuevos; la casa blanca → las casas blancas. = the new book(s); the white house(s). Learn gender with el/la.
hablar → hablante = speak → speaker; feliz → felicidad = happy → happiness; posible → imposible. Stem and accent changes are not always predictable.
¿Dónde está el libro? = Where is the book? Use opening and closing question/exclamation marks in formal writing. Spanish can omit a subject pronoun when the verb and context identify it.

sections.title: Pronunciation, spelling and noun agreement
sections.explanation:
Spanish has a comparatively stable five-vowel system; avoid reducing unstressed vowels as strongly as in English. Lexical stress is predictable from spelling rules with written accents marking exceptions and some grammatical distinctions. The tap and trill contrast in pero/perro needs targeted audio practice. Many speakers use seseo, pronouncing z and soft c like s; much of Spain distinguishes them from s with /θ/. Yeísmo and regional variants of ll/y are widespread.
Articles and adjectives agree with nouns: el problema importante, la cuestión importante, los datos nuevos. Some feminine nouns with stressed initial /a/ take el immediately before them in singular: el agua fría. They remain feminine; una, adjectives and plural forms follow the appropriate rules. Noun endings are useful clues but not guarantees: el día, la mano.
examples: el agua fría / las aguas frías
the cold water / the cold waters
Agua remains feminine even when singular el is used.
pero / perro
but / dog
A single tap contrasts with a trill in this word pair.
exercises: Correct: la problema difícil.
El problema difícil. Problema is masculine despite ending in -a.
Does seseo make a speaker’s Spanish incorrect?
No. It is standard across many Spanish-speaking communities.

sections.title: Ser, estar and past-time perspective
sections.explanation:
Ser and estar are not a simple permanent/temporary split. Ser identifies and characterises; estar often locates entities and presents states. Event location commonly uses ser: La reunión es en la biblioteca. Adjectives can change interpretation: es listo means clever; está listo means ready.
The preterite presents a bounded past event; the imperfect presents background, habit or an unfolding situation. Supe can mean found out, while sabía presents knowing as a state. The present perfect's relationship to a current time frame differs regionally; many Spain varieties use it for recent events within the current period, while many Latin American varieties prefer the preterite in more contexts. Do not mark a regional choice wrong merely because it differs from one textbook model.
examples: Cuando llegué, estaban trabajando.
When I arrived, they were working.
Preterite arrival against imperfect background.
La conferencia es mañana; el edificio está cerca.
The conference is tomorrow; the building is nearby.
Event timing with ser; entity location with estar.
exercises: Contrast era interesante and fue interesante.
The imperfect frames interest as background or ongoing description; the preterite presents the experience as bounded in context.
Translate She is ready with estar.
Está lista. Subject can be omitted when context identifies her.

sections.title: Pronouns, clitics and relative clauses
sections.explanation:
Object pronouns normally precede a finite verb and can attach to an infinitive, gerund or affirmative imperative in suitable constructions. Lo/la often mark direct objects, le indirect objects. Regional leísmo is nuanced; some uses are accepted in particular contexts, but learn a clear core system first. Before lo/la/los/las, le/les becomes se: se lo expliqué.
The personal a commonly marks specific human direct objects: vi a la profesora. It is not simply an indirect-object marker. Que is a flexible relative pronoun; quien and el cual have particular distributions, and cuyo agrees with the possessed noun: la autora cuyo libro leí. Track each pronoun's role rather than translating English who/which one-to-one.
examples: Se lo expliqué ayer.
I explained it to him/her/them yesterday.
Se replaces le/les before lo; context resolves the recipient.
La investigadora cuyo artículo leí ...
The researcher whose article I read ...
Cuyo agrees with artículo, not investigadora.
exercises: Combine le + lo in Le expliqué el problema.
Se lo expliqué. The recipient remains represented by se; lo represents the problem.
Why is vi a la profesora not automatically an indirect-object sentence?
The personal a marks a human direct object here. Ver takes the person as what was seen.

sections.title: Subjunctive, stance and relative meaning
sections.explanation:
The subjunctive appears in constructions expressing desire, evaluation, doubt, purpose and certain nonasserted situations. Espero que venga; es importante que lo sepas. Do not equate it with an event being unreal. A factual concession may use aun­que with different moods depending on how information is framed. Standard indicative assertions and subjunctive framing differ in commitment and discourse status.
Relative clauses can distinguish a known identified entity from an unspecified sought one: busco un libro que explica esto suggests an identified kind or asserted property; busco un libro que explique esto presents the desired property without asserting an available example. Cuando + subjunctive commonly refers to a future pending event. Learn triggers with their meaning and context, not an indiscriminate list.
examples: Cuando termine el informe, te lo enviaré.
When I finish the report, I will send it to you.
Future pending completion takes subjunctive in the temporal clause.
Busco una explicación que sea clara.
I am looking for an explanation that is clear.
The desired explanation is not presented as an identified existing one.
exercises: Complete: Es necesario que nosotros revis__ los datos.
Revisemos. Necessity frames the subordinate proposition in the subjunctive.
Why is subjunctive not simply imaginary grammar?
Factual content can be backgrounded or evaluated in subjunctive constructions. Mood also depends on construction and speaker stance.

sections.title: Conditionals, passive and impersonal se
sections.explanation:
Ordinary counterfactual si clauses use imperfect subjunctive with conditional: si tuviera tiempo, iría. Past counterfactuals use pluperfect subjunctive with conditional perfect: si lo hubiera sabido, habría esperado. The -ra and -se imperfect-subjunctive forms have overlapping standard uses with differences in some contexts.
The passive uses ser + participle with agreement, but se constructions are frequent. Se publicaron los resultados is a passive-like construction with plural agreement. Se entrevistó a los candidatos is impersonal with a-marked human object and singular verb in the core standard pattern. Do not assume every se sentence is reflexive. Estar + participle often describes a resulting state rather than the event passive.
examples: Si hubiéramos revisado el texto, habríamos encontrado el error.
If we had reviewed the text, we would have found the error.
Past counterfactual.
Se publicaron los resultados.
The results were published.
Plural subject agreement in a passive se construction.
exercises: Correct the ordinary conditional: Si tendría tiempo, iría.
Si tuviera tiempo, iría. Use imperfect subjunctive in the if-clause.
Contrast fue cerrado and estaba cerrado.
Fue cerrado presents a closing event in passive form; estaba cerrado presents the closed state.

sections.title: Aspectual constructions and argument connectors
sections.explanation:
Periphrases add aspect and stance: acabar de + infinitive for a recent completion in the relevant tense; seguir + gerund for continuation; volver a + infinitive for repetition; dejar de + infinitive for cessation. Their meaning is not obtained by translating each verb separately. Deber and deber de are associated with obligation and inference respectively, although actual usage overlaps.
Sin embargo contrasts; por tanto infers; aun así concedes despite a preceding point; en cambio sets a contrasting comparison. Spanish academic prose often allows long sentences, but clarity still depends on clause boundaries and explicit references. Use collocations such as plantear una hipótesis, llevar a cabo un estudio and llegar a una conclusión.
examples: El equipo sigue revisando los datos.
The team is continuing to review the data.
Seguir + gerund marks continuation.
Los resultados son prometedores; aun así, hace falta confirmarlos.
The results are promising; even so, they need confirmation.
Concession prevents an overstrong conclusion.
exercises: Express We stopped using that method.
Dejamos de usar ese método. Dejar de marks cessation.
Replace Esto prueba todo with a limited claim.
Estos datos apoyan la hipótesis, pero no descartan otras explicaciones. The conclusion stays evidentially limited.

sections.title: Advanced reading and discourse analysis
sections.explanation:
Original teaching passage: Una explicación puede resultar convincente sin que los datos disponibles la confirmen de manera concluyente. Por ello, conviene distinguir entre lo que se observa y lo que se infiere. Cuanto más claramente se describan las condiciones del estudio, más fácil será evaluar el alcance de sus conclusiones. Reconocer una limitación no equivale a rechazar todo el análisis.
Translation: An explanation can be convincing without the available data confirming it conclusively. Therefore, it is appropriate to distinguish what is observed from what is inferred. The more clearly the study conditions are described, the easier it will be to assess the scope of its conclusions. Recognising a limitation does not amount to rejecting the whole analysis.
Sin que introduces subjunctive; la points back to explicación. Lo que creates a neutral nominal relative. Alcance denotes scope. No equivale a blocks a false equivalence. Analyse the logical roles before making a fluent paraphrase.
examples: sin que los datos la confirmen
without the data confirming it
Subjunctive after sin que; la refers to explicación.
no equivale a rechazar todo el análisis
does not amount to rejecting the whole analysis
Equivaler a licenses an infinitive complement here.
exercises: What is the passage’s central distinction?
Observed data and inferred explanations must be separated; persuasiveness is not conclusive confirmation.
Write a 150-word summary and a 150-word objection.
Preserve the author’s scope in the summary. In the objection, criticise a precise assumption and distinguish it from your own claim.

sections.title: Regional competence, idiom and advanced production
sections.explanation:
Recognise vosotros conjugation in Spain and ustedes in most of Latin America. Voseo has several regional systems and should be studied from a specific community's models, not assumed to have one universal conjugation. Differences in vocabulary can be neutral, affectionate or offensive depending on region. Verify context before imitating a colloquial expression.
Advanced production requires more than subjunctive accuracy. Study conventional openings, hedging, irony, indirect criticism, conversational turn-taking and natural collocations. Compare an informal voice note with an academic paragraph expressing the same idea. Avoid excessive literal translations of English passive sentences or pronoun subjects where Spanish discourse normally omits them.
examples: ¿Podría aclarar este punto?
Could you clarify this point?
A conventional courteous professional request.
En fin, habrá que revisarlo otra vez.
Well/anyway, it will have to be reviewed again.
Discourse meaning and impersonal necessity depend on context.
exercises: What should a regional-expression note contain?
Community, context, register, meaning, an authentic example and any offensive or misleading interpretation elsewhere.
Revise a formal paragraph into natural conversation.
Preserve the facts while reducing dense nominalisations and adjusting connectors, address and sentence length. Obtain feedback on naturalness.

rules.title: Articles and gender
rules.explanation: Articles agree in gender and number. Learn el/la with the noun. El can also occur before a stressed initial a sound in some feminine singular nouns; the noun remains feminine.

examples.native: No han igualado la carretera.
examples.translation: The road hasn't been leveled.

examples.native: Yo tengo un anillo.
examples.translation: I have a ring.

examples.native: Hay un ratón en la despensa.
examples.translation: There's a mouse in the pantry.

rules.title: Adjective agreement
rules.explanation: Most adjectives agree with the noun. Some change only for number. Position and shortened forms can affect meaning: un buen libro versus el libro es bueno.

examples.native: Ésta si que va a ser buena.
examples.translation: This is going to be swell.

examples.native: No puedo dejarte desembarcar sin darte un beso grande.
examples.translation: I can't let you disembark without giving you a big kiss.

examples.native: Los abejorros son más grandes que las abejas.
examples.translation: Bumblebees are bigger than bees.

rules.title: Ser forms
rules.explanation: Ser identifies or characterises a referent and expresses many classifications. Do not reduce the distinction to permanent versus temporary; events and time also use ser.

examples.native: ¿Es ésta tu cartera?
examples.translation: Is this your wallet?

examples.native: Ésas no son vuestras sillas.
examples.translation: Those are not your chairs.

examples.native: Uno es juzgado por su forma de hablar en primera instancia.
examples.translation: One is judged by one's speech first of all.

rules.title: Estar forms
rules.explanation: Estar commonly locates entities and describes states or results. The same adjective with ser and estar can express different meanings. Estar plus gerund marks an ongoing situation.

examples.native: Tomás también está nervioso.
examples.translation: Tom is nervous, too.

examples.native: ¿Qué estáis haciendo vosotros dos?
examples.translation: What are you two doing?

examples.native: Estoy viendo la casa.
examples.translation: I see the house.

rules.title: Existence with haber
rules.explanation: Impersonal haber states existence: hay un libro. It normally remains singular in standard usage even with a plural following noun. It differs from locating a known referent with estar.

examples.native: Tom le dijo a Mary lo que había pasado.
examples.translation: Tom told Mary what had happened.

examples.native: No hay escapatoria.
examples.translation: There is no escape.

examples.native: Tom se preguntó qué le había pasado a Mary.
examples.translation: Tom wondered what happened to Mary.

rules.title: Present possession
rules.explanation: Tener agrees with the subject and expresses possession. It also occurs in expressions such as tener hambre and tener que + infinitive. Spanish often omits an understood subject pronoun.

examples.native: Él tiene mucho pegue.
examples.translation: He's got lots of sex appeal.

examples.native: No tienen ningún impacto sobre el ambiente.
examples.translation: They have no impact on the environment.

examples.native: ¿Cuánto tiempo tengo que quedarme aquí?
examples.translation: How long do I have to stay here?

rules.title: Past background
rules.explanation: The imperfect typically presents background, a past state or a habit. A preterite presents an event as bounded in its narrative frame. The difference is viewpoint, not a simple long/short duration rule.

examples.native: Ella estaba profundamente emocionada.
examples.translation: She was deeply moved.

examples.native: Los antiguos egipcios creían que el Sol era el ojo del dios Ra.
examples.translation: The ancient Egyptians believed that the Sun was the eye of the god Ra.

examples.native: Cuando mi madre era joven, era muy guapa.
examples.translation: When my mother was young, she was very beautiful.

rules.title: Bounded past forms
rules.explanation: The preterite presents past events as bounded. Fue may be a form of ser or ir; context determines the verb. Common irregular forms need direct practice in sentences.

examples.native: Él me dio todo pero no aceptó nada a cambio.
examples.translation: He gave me everything but took nothing in return.

examples.native: La primera máquina imprenta fue inventada por Gutenberg.
examples.translation: The first printing machine was invented by Gutenberg.

examples.native: Le picó una avispa y tuvo una reacción alérgica.
examples.translation: A wasp stung him and he had an allergic reaction.

rules.title: Subjunctive forms
rules.explanation: Subjunctive selection depends on a governing expression and the status of the proposition. Wishes, evaluation, negation and non-specific relatives often matter. It is not merely a marker of anything uncertain.

examples.native: «Quiero que mi elfo oscuro sea azul.» «De acuerdo... Ése es morado. Serás morado esta semana.»
examples.translation: "I want my dark elf to be blue." "OK... That one's purple. You'll be purple for this week."

examples.native: Recojan tantas monedas como sea posible.
examples.translation: Collect as many coins as possible.

examples.native: No creo que esto sea gracioso.
examples.translation: I don't think this is funny.

rules.title: Conditional forms
rules.explanation: The conditional can express a hypothetical result or politeness. A common unreal present pattern is si + imperfect subjunctive followed by conditional.

examples.native: Por favor, ¿Podría canjear estos cheques de viaje?
examples.translation: Would you cash these travelers checks, please?

examples.native: Si fuera invisible no tendría que vestirme.
examples.translation: If I were invisible I wouldn't have to dress myself.

examples.native: Con tus habilidades, estoy seguro de que no te sería muy difícil encontrar otro trabajo.
examples.translation: With your skills, I'm sure it wouldn't be too hard to find another job.

rules.title: Progressive constructions
rules.explanation: Estar + gerund focuses on an ongoing action. Spanish does not use the progressive in all situations where English does. A gerund can also appear with other verbs or as an adverbial.

examples.native: «Solo estaba hablando con él.» «¿Hablando con él de qué?» «Eso no es asunto tuyo.»
examples.translation: "I was just talking to him." "Talking to him about what?" "That's none of your business."

examples.native: ¿Por qué Tom sigue haciendo eso?
examples.translation: Why's Tom still doing that?

examples.native: Como muchos de los estudiantes de nuestra escuela, Tom se queda despierto hasta tarde en la noche estudiando.
examples.translation: Like many students at our school, Tom stays up until late at night studying.

rules.title: Object pronouns
rules.explanation: Lo/la/los/las generally mark direct objects; le/les generally mark indirect objects. Regional leísmo complicates some personal direct objects. Before lo/la/los/las, an indirect le/les becomes se.

examples.native: Tom no le creyó a Mary.
examples.translation: Tom didn't believe Mary.

examples.native: Ha de haber alguna razón por lo que ha hecho.
examples.translation: There must be some reason for what he has done.

examples.native: Me siento totalmente fuera de lugar.
examples.translation: I feel so out of place.

rules.title: Reflexive and other se
rules.explanation: Se can mark reflexivity, reciprocal action, an impersonal/passive-like construction or an indirect object before a direct clitic. Decide from the verb and participants rather than treating all se alike.

examples.native: Tom se bebió un vaso de leche.
examples.translation: Tom drank a glass of milk.

examples.native: ¿Qué se puede encontrar más allá del final del universo?
examples.translation: What can be found beyond the end of the universe?

examples.native: ¿Como se dice eso en cabilio?
examples.translation: What's it called in Kabyle?

rules.title: Relative words
rules.explanation: Relative words connect a clause to a referent. Cuyo agrees with the possessed noun, not the possessor. Que also introduces complement clauses; compare functions in the whole sentence.

examples.native: No puedo, a pesar que quiero.
examples.translation: I can't even if I want to.

examples.native: No puedo creer que Tom aceptara nuestra oferta.
examples.translation: I can't believe Tom accepted our offer.

examples.native: Tuve que ir ahí solo.
examples.translation: I had to go there alone.

rules.title: Negation
rules.explanation: Spanish permits negative concord: No vi a nadie. A negative word before the verb normally makes a separate no unnecessary: Nadie vino. Concord does not cancel the negative meaning.

examples.native: Esa clase de cosas no puede encontrarse en cualquier parte.
examples.translation: That kind of thing can't be found just anywhere.

examples.native: No nací sabiendo.
examples.translation: I wasn't born knowing.

examples.native: Si tú no vas a esquiar, yo tampoco iré.
examples.translation: If you don't go skiing, I won't, either.

rules.title: Question words
rules.explanation: Question and exclamation words take written accents, including many indirect questions. Compare donde as a relative with dónde in a question. Use the opening question mark in standard writing.

examples.native: ¿Por qué estabas enfadado conmigo?
examples.translation: Why were you angry with me?

examples.native: ¿Qué quieres decir con relativismo cultural?
examples.translation: What do you mean by cultural relativism?

examples.native: ¿Qué saben ustedes?
examples.translation: What do you know?

rules.title: Conditions with si
rules.explanation: Si has no accent when it means if or whether; sí means yes or emphatic affirmation. A real condition often uses present; an unreal one often uses imperfect subjunctive.

examples.native: Si yo hubiera sabido su dirección, le habría mandado una carta.
examples.translation: If I had known her address, I would have written to her.

examples.native: Léela tú misma, si quieres.
examples.translation: Read it yourself, if you like.

examples.native: Si te agachas un poco, verás la bandera de señalización apareciendo y ocultándose de la vista.
examples.translation: If you just crouch a little, the signal flag can just be seen flicking in and out of sight.

rules.title: Cause and concession
rules.explanation: Porque supplies a reason; aunque introduces concession; por eso supplies a consequence. Aunque can take indicative or subjunctive according to how its content is presented.

examples.native: A la gente no le gusta trabajar con Tom porque es difícil llevarse bien con él.
examples.translation: People don't like working with Tom because he's hard to get along with.

examples.native: Ya que estamos todos de acuerdo, empecemos la reunión.
examples.translation: Now we all agree, let's start the meeting.

examples.native: No te tienes que sentir mal por eso.
examples.translation: You don't have to feel bad for that.

rules.title: Contractions and prepositions
rules.explanation: Al contracts a + el and del contracts de + el. Por and para encode different relationships, including route/cause versus purpose/recipient in common uses. Learn contrasts in complete phrases.

examples.native: Pruébalo por favor.
examples.translation: Please have a try.

examples.native: ¿Estarías de acuerdo con eso?
examples.translation: Would you agree with that?

examples.native: Esta tarde voy a jugar con Naoko.
examples.translation: I will play with Naoko this afternoon.

rules.title: Comparison
rules.explanation: Más/menos ... que compare. Tan ... como compares a quality; tanto ... como compares quantity and may require agreement. Mejor and peor are common irregular comparatives.

examples.native: Cuanto peor mejor.
examples.translation: The worse the better.

examples.native: Sé tan poco como tú.
examples.translation: I know as little as you do.

examples.native: Hasta un niño chico sabe algo tan simple.
examples.translation: The smallest child knows such a simple thing.

passages.title: Learning with a clear purpose
passages.native: Estoy aprendiendo un idioma nuevo. Cada día leo un texto corto y escucho ejemplos claros. Escribo palabras útiles en un cuaderno. Cuando cometo un error, reviso la regla y lo intento de nuevo. Mi objetivo es comprender a las personas y expresar mis ideas con claridad.
passages.translation: I am learning a new language. Each day, I read a short text and listen to clear examples. I write useful words in a notebook. When I make a mistake, I check the rule and try again. My goal is to understand people and express my ideas clearly.

passages.title: Art: interpretation and context
passages.native: Una obra puede admitir varias interpretaciones sin que todas estén igualmente justificadas. El lector o espectador debe prestar atención a los detalles de la obra, a su contexto y a las razones que ofrece cada interpretación. La intención del creador puede ser relevante, pero no siempre resuelve todas las preguntas. También importa distinguir una reacción personal de una afirmación sobre lo que la obra expresa. Una discusión cuidadosa permite comparar lecturas diferentes sin reducirlas a una sola respuesta ni aceptar cualquier explicación sin argumentos.
passages.guide: A work can support several interpretations without all being equally justified. The reader or viewer should consider details, context and reasons. The creator's intention may matter without resolving every question. A personal reaction differs from a claim about what the work expresses. Careful discussion compares interpretations without forcing one answer or accepting unsupported explanations.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
